claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a single-phase solid solution with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Demanding mechanical loading produces localized compositional fluctuations in the alloy.
Localized compositional fluctuations trigger strain-induced short-range ordering or precipitation.
The load-induced ordered regions or precipitates are brittle intermetallic phases.
Nanoscale precipitates or ordered clusters preferentially form at regions of accumulated strain and stress concentration.
Mechanical loading creates local stress concentrations that promote elemental segregation.
Load-induced elemental segregation triggers phase decomposition into intermetallic or ordered regions.
The precipitates or ordered regions act as crack-nucleation sites.
Crack nucleation at the precipitates or ordered regions degrades toughness and leads to brittle fracture under further loading.
Demanding loading without a suppression treatment will reduce fracture strain relative to the initial baseline.
Demanding loading without a suppression treatment will decrease fracture energy absorption relative to the initial baseline.
A post-load thermal treatment that mitigates ordering will improve retention of ductility and toughness relative to loaded, untreated samples.
High-strain-rate or cyclic loading at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures activates load-induced diffusion and segregation.
The proposed mechanism may not operate under low-stress, long-term static conditions.
A rapid quench or stabilization anneal can suppress diffusion-driven ordering in loaded samples.
